tactics.claim: Never discount the core offer to close a deal — add bonuses instead, because discounting teaches customers your prices are negotiable.
tactics.mechanism: A concession on price is remembered as a precedent, so future purchases are made in anticipation of a discount. Adding value keeps the price anchor intact and puts the seller in a position of strength.
tactics.evidence: Assertion presented as a pro-tip. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable and correct for this business, but it restates two things already in place: offer-construction's 'stop equating offer with discount' opener and its 'prefer adding good stuff over removing cost' framing rule, plus the win-back note about not training the list to wait for sales.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicates existing offer-construction framing rules; the concrete substitution it implies is already carried by the bonus-with-urgency tactic adopted above.

tactics.claim: Get adjacent non-competing businesses to contribute their products and services as bonuses in exchange for exposure to your customers, then negotiate group discounts and referral commissions so the bonuses become revenue streams.
tactics.mechanism: Your customer list is the currency: partners get free access to pre-qualified buyers, you get high-value bonuses at zero cost, and referral commissions can turn the bonus stack into profit on top of the core sale.
tactics.evidence: Detailed pain-clinic worked example (massage, chiro, food discounts, gym, pharmacy) totalling more than the $400 offer price, plus his Prestige Labs sponsored-athlete discount-and-commission arrangement. Anecdotal.

rscFit.reasoning: The mechanism prices exposure to your customer base as the bargaining chip, and at ~54 orders/month with a list too small to run a personalized win-back, RSC has nothing a partner would trade real product or a commission for.

tactics.rejectReason: Requires audience scale RSC lacks and adds partner negotiation and tracking load to a solo operator, on the wrong side of the gated sequence.

tactics.claim: Make a habit of recording every workshop, webinar, event and interview so you accumulate a vault of bonus assets to sprinkle into offers as needed.
tactics.mechanism: One-time recorded content has high perceived value, near-zero marginal cost, and zero operational effort beyond granting a login, so a growing library gives you objection-crushing bonuses on demand.
tactics.evidence: Author's note that the longer you are in business the more of these assets you accumulate; assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: The assets described are artifacts of a service and information business — workshops, webinars, events — none of which RSC runs or has reason to run.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicates the adopted create-once-asset tactic while pointing a solo body-care operator at content production instead of the CRO and Offer work the sequence calls for.

tactics.claim: Reversing risk is the single highest-leverage way to make any offer more attractive — identify the buyer's biggest fear, turn it into the guarantee, and state it boldly with a reason why.
tactics.mechanism: Risk that the product won't work is the biggest objection to any purchase and the unspoken fear is what blocks the sale, so whatever position you take on risk should be stated loudly rather than buried; experienced marketers spend as much time on the guarantee as on the deliverables.
tactics.evidence: Assertion supported by the secondhand Fladlien claim of 2-4x conversion changes from guarantee quality, plus the diagnostic prompt 'what do they not want to have happen if they pay you?'

rscFit.reasoning: Durable and well-fitted to the category, but marketing-offer-construction already owns risk reversal — naming the buyer's single biggest fear, guaranteeing against it, building the cost into price, and moving the promise out of the footer to where the buyer decides.

tactics.rejectReason: Headline claim duplicates an existing offer-construction tactic; the additive material (conditional structure, refund math, COGS caution, naming) is captured as separate tactics above.

tactics.claim: Use an 'anti-guarantee' — explicitly state that all sales are final, justified by how exclusive, powerful, and easily copied the thing is, inventing a compelling reason why if needed.
tactics.mechanism: Because guarantees are near-universal, the absence of one is attention-worthy; framing it as a damaging admission ('once seen it cannot be unseen') implies the product works so well that offering a refund would expose you, and it removes abuse exposure on goods you cannot resell.
tactics.evidence: Examples of easily-stolen information products (a checkout code, cold-outreach scripts) plus a suggested script and the instruction to 'just make one up that sounds compelling.' Assertion, no evidence of outperformance.

rscFit.reasoning: Directional mismatch: RSC's binding constraint is retention and the known churn cause is a first-time buyer concluding during the transition period that natural deodorant failed, so an all-sales-final stance argues the opposite of the conditional transition-period guarantee. It is also unavailable on Amazon where returns are platform-controlled and prominent.

tactics.rejectReason: Contradicts the source's own low-ticket-B2C guidance and the adopted transition-period guarantee, is unavailable on the larger channel, and the instruction to fabricate a reason why is a compliance and trust hazard in body care.

tactics.claim: Use implied guarantees — performance-based pay, revenue share, profit share, ratchets, and bonus triggers — so you only get paid if the client gets results.
tactics.mechanism: Tying compensation to a measurable outcome removes the buyer's risk entirely, weeds out low performers, and creates a collaborative long-term relationship; the drawbacks are tracking and collection.
tactics.evidence: Listed as one of four guarantee types with named structures, plus claims of seeing 'countless agencies go from $20k/mo to $200k+/mo in a matter of a few months' after switching from retainer to performance. No named cases or figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Applies only to service and performance engagements where an outcome is jointly measured and payment can be contingent. A $12 physical deodorant sold on Shopify and Amazon has no measurable client outcome, no post-delivery billing relationship, and no mechanism for contingent payment.

tactics.rejectReason: B2B service-pricing model with no honest translation to a consumable catalog, and it depends on tracking/attribution that does not yet exist.

tactics.claim: Stack multiple guarantees — for example an unconditional 30-day no-questions guarantee on top of a conditional 90-day triple-your-money-back guarantee, or two sequential conditional outcomes.
tactics.mechanism: Layering guarantees future-paces the prospect into believing the outcome is far more likely, because you are spelling out specific results with timelines and putting money behind each one.
tactics.evidence: Assertion illustrated with a $10,000-by-60-days / $30,000-by-90-days coaching example. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Mismatched in magnitude: at a $50.46 AOV on a consumable a triple-money-back layer is real cash out of a ~$2,700/mo operation, and multiple stacked promises crowd the above-the-fold space the adopted information-fatigue rule protects. The examples are multi-thousand-dollar coaching milestones with no deodorant analogue.

tactics.rejectReason: Payout magnitude is unaffordable and the single conditional transition-period guarantee already adopted captures all the usable effect.

tactics.claim: Deliver an unconditional guarantee with the 'fully informed decision' script — reframe the buy as getting inside to evaluate, promise a refund for any reason whatsoever, and name the support address and response time.
tactics.mechanism: Reframing the purchase as information-gathering rather than commitment removes the decision from the moment of the pitch, and naming the exact refund channel plus response time proves the promise is real rather than theoretical.
tactics.evidence: A verbatim Jason Fladlien webinar pitch reproduced in full; presented as 'unbelievable' but with no conversion figures attached.

rscFit.reasoning: It is a spoken webinar close for an information product delivered by login, where refunds cost nothing and the buyer can genuinely 'get inside and look'. A physical consumable has no inside to look at, and an any-reason refund on a used deodorant returns nothing sellable while eating postage twice.

tactics.rejectReason: Format and refund economics do not transfer to physical goods; the one portable fragment (state the refund process and where to ask, plainly) is already owned by the returns-and-cancellation-terms tactic in marketing-conversion-friction-audit.

tactics.claim: Match the guarantee type to your ticket size and buyer type — broad, unconditional satisfaction guarantees work best for lower-ticket B2C, while higher-ticket or B2B offers should use specific, conditional guarantees.
tactics.mechanism: On low-ticket consumer purchases most buyers never bother to claim, so a maximally generous promise buys a large conversion lift at a small realized refund cost; as ticket and fulfillment cost rise, the same promise becomes expensive, so conditions and specificity are needed to keep it affordable.
tactics.evidence: Reports using an unconditional satisfaction guarantee selling weight-loss programs with only two claims out of 4,000 sales in three and a half years; the low-ticket-vs-high-ticket rule stated as practitioner judgment with no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable principle class and the selection rule the existing guarantee tactic lacks: RSC is exactly the case the source says should go broadest — low-ticket B2C consumables at a $50.46 AOV, where the redemption cost of a no-questions 30-day promise is bounded and the CRO/Offer stage is reachable with zero spend. It also warns against over-engineering conditions on a $12 deodorant. Not higher because Amazon (~$1,800/mo) already gives buyers a generous platform return policy, so incremental lift concentrates on the ~$875/mo Shopify side, and refund cost is real cash at this revenue level.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add the guarantee-selection rule: low-ticket B2C should offer the broadest, simplest promise (few or no conditions), reserving specific conditional guarantees for high-ticket or high-fulfilment-cost offers.

tactics.claim: Use a delayed-second-payment guarantee: don't bill the customer again until they have reached their first concrete outcome.
tactics.mechanism: Removing the second charge until a result lands eliminates the buyer's fear of paying repeatedly for something that isn't working, and it forces the seller to concentrate on activation — the first-result milestone that predicts long-term retention.
tactics.evidence: Stated as a personal favorite used 'loads of times', with examples (lose your first five pounds, make your first sale, get your website live); anecdotal, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: It translates to the one recurring-revenue surface RSC has: a subscribe-and-save enrollment where the second shipment is timed to land after the transition period, stated as 'you won't be billed again until you're through the switch — cancel free before then.' That addresses the commitment fear blocking subscription enrollment, the binding retention constraint, and costs nothing beyond a subscription-app interval setting plus copy. Held at 6 because a physical shipment isn't a service — the second charge funds inventory already sent — so the honest implementation is a longer first interval plus an explicit free-cancel window, and Amazon offers no such control.

targetSkill.name: marketing-retention-offers
targetSkill.description: Add: time the second subscription charge to land after the activation milestone (the transition period) and say so plainly with a free-cancel window, so the commitment fear does not block enrollment.

tactics.claim: Name the offer with the M-A-G-I-C components — a magnetic reason why, an announced avatar, a goal (dream outcome), a time interval, and a container word that signals a system rather than a commodity — using three to five of them in whatever order sounds punchiest.
tactics.mechanism: Prospects judge the offer by its cover: the same underlying thing converts at wildly different rates depending on its name ('Free Six-Week Stress Release Challenge' vs. 'Float Tank Center Session'). Each component answers a question the buyer has before clicking — why now, is this for me, what result, how long, is this a real system — so a name carrying several of them pre-sells before any body copy is read, at zero change to delivery cost, while repelling the wrong buyer.
tactics.evidence: The float-tank vs. stress-release-challenge comparison plus roughly 25 worked example names across wellness, dental, chiropractic, and coaching ('Free Six-Week Lean-By-Halloween Challenge', '88% Off 12-Week Bikini Blueprint'). Claims of 2x/3x/10x response lift are assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable positioning/offer-construction principle and the concrete formula layer under the existing 'name every tier deliberately' tactic: goal + interval + container turns a vague bundle into 'The 30-Day Natural Switch Kit' or 'Transition-Proof 3-Pack' on a Shopify bundle page, a collection tile, an Amazon multipack title, and an email subject line — exactly the naming work that makes an already-listed multipack sell and lifts AOV above $50.46 at zero cost. Not higher because the avatar/hyper-local guidance is irrelevant to a national catalog, challenge/bootcamp container words need swapping for kit/system/routine/reset, the claim-plus-duration ad-policy note is suspect, and the lift is unmeasurable at ~54 orders/month.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add the offer-naming formula: combine three to five of reason-why, avatar, desired outcome, time interval, and a container word (kit, system, routine, reset) when naming bundles, collections, and multipack listings.

tactics.claim: When an offer stops working, change things in a fixed order from lightest to heaviest — creative, then body copy, then the headline/wrapper (name and seasonal framing), then duration, then the free/discount enhancer, and only as a last resort the monetization structure and price points — leaving products, pricing, and deliverables unchanged for as long as possible.
tactics.mechanism: What fatigues is the market's familiarity with the presentation, not the underlying value, and the top of the list is cheap and repeatable while the bottom is operationally heavy. Re-skinning the same offer restores novelty without the cost or risk of rebuilding the product, price, or fulfillment behind it, so one working offer can be run indefinitely.
tactics.evidence: Worked wrapper swaps ('Six-Week Stress Release Challenge' → '42-Day Relaxing Holidays Challenge', 'Holiday Hangover' → 'New Year New You'), the assertion that when ads fatigue 'we don't change our entire business, we just run the same ad again with a different image', plus local-market media-cost arithmetic and a disclaimer that fatigue happens over years, not months.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable change-ordering discipline whose real value here is as a brake: when Shopify revenue sits at ~$875/mo the reflex is to reformulate, add SKU 13, or cut price, and this says re-skin the wrapper first (Amazon main image, PDP hero, bundle name, seasonal framing) before touching structure — reinforcing the adopted 'add ways to offer, not products' gate. Capped at 6 because the top two rungs are ad creative and ad body copy, which do not exist here (paid is gated), so RSC enters at rung three, and the fatigue mechanism it was written for (paid-reach saturation) is premature at this traffic level — retention, not fatigue, is the diagnosis.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add the lightest-to-heaviest change ladder: refresh imagery, copy, name, and seasonal wrapper before touching duration, enhancers, price, or product structure when an offer underperforms.

tactics.claim: Guarantee the outcome rather than the refund — keep working for free until the client achieves the result, or cover their ancillary costs (hotel, airfare, hourly wage, ad spend) until they do.
tactics.mechanism: Guaranteeing the outcome instead of the money eliminates refund exposure while making the promise feel stronger; the seller only risks time, and in practice almost nobody claims because clients who do the work get close enough to be satisfied.
tactics.evidence: Claims never to have had a client take up the service guarantee; the wage-payment guarantee framed as one 'you will never actually have to give out.' Anecdotal.

rscFit.reasoning: Every variant assumes ongoing labor the seller can extend for free — coaching calls, one-on-one work, reimbursed travel or ad spend. A solo operator shipping a $12 consumable has no free labor to extend, no defined client outcome to guarantee, and no ancillary costs to cover.

tactics.rejectReason: No service labour or client outcome exists to guarantee; there is no honest translation to a deodorant SKU.

tactics.claim: Make offer names rhyme or alliterate so they stick in buyers' minds.
tactics.mechanism: Rhyme and alliteration improve memorability and recall of the offer name.
tactics.evidence: Example names ('Six-Pack Fast Track', 'Debt Detox', 'Big Booty Bootcamp') with the caveat not to force it. Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable and free, but a cosmetic sub-detail of the naming formula already being adopted, with no independent mechanism beyond memorability — and memorability is not the constraint at ~54 orders/month; retention is.

tactics.rejectReason: Cosmetic sub-detail of the adopted naming formula; keeping it separately would dilute the naming guidance rather than sharpen it.

tactics.claim: Apply the same naming formula to every sub-item and bonus inside the stack, not just to the offer as a whole.
tactics.mechanism: Each named component reads as a distinct thing of value that resonates with the prospect, so the perceived value of the bundle rises above the sum of generically-labelled parts without adding any cost or SKU.
tactics.evidence: Stated as a 'Pro Tip'; assertion only, no examples or data.

rscFit.reasoning: Purely editorial and zero cost for a solo operator, with an obvious concrete form across a 12-SKU catalog: the multipack becomes a named kit whose parts are named too ('the Transition Guide', 'the Pit Reset Bar', 'the 8-Week Refill'), raising perceived value of the bundle that is already the adopted AOV lever and of the packaging insert / routine already adopted for retention. Not higher because naming alone moves no revenue if the bundle economics are wrong, and the effect cannot be read at ~54 orders/month.

targetSkill.name: marketing-offer-construction
targetSkill.description: Add: name every component inside a bundle, not just the bundle — each named part reads as a distinct item of value at no added cost or SKU.

tactics.claim: Run two or three of your best offer names in the ad campaign, quickly note the winner, then treat it as the control to test new names against.
tactics.mechanism: Name performance is unpredictable, so head-to-head testing rather than reasoning identifies the winner, and holding a control prevents you from replacing a proven name with a worse one.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, plus the admission 'I honestly have no idea why some names win and others do not.'

rscFit.reasoning: Depends on scale that does not exist: the named test surface is an advertising campaign, which is gated behind Tracking → CRO → Offer/AOV → Traffic, and at ~54 orders/month with broken attribution no name-versus-name comparison will reach a readable signal.

tactics.rejectReason: Test mechanism is unexecutable at this volume and would produce false confidence; the naming principle itself is adopted separately.

tactics.claim: Build several proven offers so you can rotate between them at will — multiple 'aces in the hole' keep marketing converting at a higher level, provided rotation doesn't create operational drag.
tactics.mechanism: Markets fatigue on a single offer, so alternating between offers that have each already been shown to convert keeps response rates high without inventing anything new.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, framed as 'the ultimate position of power'; no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Presumes a saturated audience and a library of validated offers. At ~$2,700/mo across Shopify and Amazon the same offer has not been seen enough times to fatigue, and there is no proven offer yet to rotate against; rotating bundles across 12 SKUs also adds inventory and listing work — the drag the source itself warns about.

tactics.rejectReason: Preconditions (audience saturation, a library of proven offers) do not exist; the binding constraint is retention, not offer freshness.

tactics.claim: Local businesses must variate offers, headlines, and creative rapidly because a small service radius means a small TAM, so offers fatigue fast.
tactics.mechanism: Fatigue rate is a function of addressable market size — the smaller the radius, the sooner everyone has seen the offer.
tactics.evidence: Personal experience running local businesses; anecdotal.

rscFit.reasoning: Targets a business model RSC does not operate: there is no service radius, revenue comes from national Shopify and Amazon ecommerce, so the TAM-driven fatigue mechanic does not apply.

tactics.rejectReason: Local-business model mismatch; no service radius and none of the in-person trust advantages it trades on.

tactics.claim: Don't be emotional about naming results — keep trying, keep striking out, try more, and you'll get there; your first Grand Slam Offer should get you to your first $100,000.
tactics.mechanism: Persistence through failed attempts eventually produces a winner because entrepreneurship is about acquiring skills, beliefs, and character traits.
tactics.evidence: Personal story about hitting $101,018 in personal savings in March 2017, plus a Charlie Munger epigraph.

rscFit.reasoning: Motivational framing with no stated mechanism — nothing to execute, nothing to test, no artifact or surface it touches.

tactics.rejectReason: Non-actionable motivational framing.
